description: We are a group of passionate students from North Carolina who love citrus fruits.
summary:
On June 18th, 2017, in Pedrógão Grande, Portugal, a wildfire was seen by two NASA satellites. 35 minutes after MODIS recorded 35 hot spots, VIIRS saw 239. MODIS flew from 2001, while VIIRS took over in 2012. Stitched together, fire quadrupled, though only the instruments changed.

Now, MODIS is ending, so its 2001 to 2011 data can’t be compared with today’s. Fire Ledger translates those years into today’s scale. Using 2012 - 2019, when both satellites were active, our model learned to map MODIS to VIIRS, accounting for fire intensity, regional activity, season, time of day, and latitude. It converts every MODIS year into VIIRS’ scale with an uncertainty band, and using NOAA-20/21, we carry these records up to last week. We proved this by hiding 2020 through 2025 from the model and predicting them: for Ghana, our model had a 4.3% error versus 6.8% for a single fixed ratio. And NASA’s independent burned-area data agrees, as the 2012 jump falls from 4.56x to 1.04x. We ran this in every country with enough fire, and it won in 92 of 176 countries.

In Ghana, the stitched data shows a rise of 5.1% per year, while harmonized fires dropped 1.1%. Fire managers and scientists can now ask whether this month is unusual and why. Explore 176 countries on an interactive globe, a monthly burn calendar, NASA imagery of any month, and downloadable data, built on FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS, MCD64 burned area, POWER, and SRTM.
details:
Our project, Fire Ledger, is a collection of features intended to help scientists, firefighters, and the public make crucial decisions about fire hotspots. Its foundation is the harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS data, to show more accurately how the concentration of fire hotspots has changed over time, but it has grown to include a suite of utilities and additional visualization and computational features to further help these groups. The primary method for harmonizing 176 countries’ fire hotspot data was a standardized Poisson regression model that maps MODIS data onto VIIRS. It was trained on data from 2012 to 2019, when both satellite instruments were collecting data, and learns from their side-by-side counts. The unit is one grid cell (0.25 degrees; coarser for big countries, up to 8 degrees, so that each has at most 400 burning cells). The model is refitted on resampled data, giving a 5–95% uncertainty band. Its performance is then validated on 2020–2025, years hidden during training: it predicts them from MODIS values alone, and the predictions are checked against what VIIRS actually counted. To quantify trends, we computed the Theil–Sen slope and the Mann–Kendall significance test, and then checked independently against NASA MCD64 burned area to see whether the jump is still present. As noted above, although this model was our main contribution, we implemented various other features for visualization and computation, listed below:

  • Landing story: a scroll-driven story over a Blender-rendered scene of the 2017 central Portugal fires. It explains how the satellites see fire and why their counts need harmonizing, then ends on the burn calendar. It shows the problem: Aqua MODIS counted 35 hot pixels, and Suomi NPP VIIRS counted 239 just 35 minutes later.
  • Feature tiles: links from under the hero section to the main features. Each tile has its own live number.
  • 3D globe (/globe): spin a globe of every country with a fire record, and color it by a single year or by the trend since 2001. Play through the years, or click a country to see its numbers. A sortable table below it lists every place with its observed trend and a label.
  • Ledger (/ledger): the harmonized fire record for a region, with a region switcher, a date range, and a plain-language trend summary. A method card explains how the record was built and how far to trust it. The Raw-to-Harmonized switch shows Ghana’s ×4.1 jump in 2012, caused by the change in collection methods, disappearing when the 2001–2011 data are back-cast to the VIIRS scale with a 5–95% band, so that our predictions are not presented as definite facts.
  • Record labels: every ledger (3 regions + 176 countries) is labelled as a model, a model with a caveat (the band held in fewer than 4 of the 6 hold-out years), a constant-ratio estimate, or too sparse, along with the reason.
  • Trend tests: the 2001–2025 trend on the stitched and harmonized records is tested with a 90% interval. For example, in Ghana the stitched record rises 5.1% a year while the harmonized record falls 1.1% a year, and both are significant.
  • This fire season so far: the latest season’s running total of fire, drawn over every past season, so you can see whether this year is running ahead or behind. It ranks the season and forecasts the season’s total with a 5–95% range that is back-tested on 25 seasons. For NW India, the range held in 21 of 25 seasons.
  • When each season burns: the days on which each past season reached 10%, 50%, and 90% of its fire, showing whether seasons start or peak earlier than they used to.
  • Burn calendar (/calendar): one square per month since 2001, all on one scale, so bad and quiet seasons stand out at a glance. Each region gets a line on fire weather (dry air, wind, rain) from NASA POWER. A month/week switch shows weekly counts as well. A “This month so far” section compares the running month with the same days in past years, alongside the NASA POWER fire-weather percentile.
  • Listen to the calendar: plays the calendar as sound, one note per month, with higher notes meaning more fire. A short tour plays the raw and harmonized counts around the 2012 satellite change, so you can hear the jump that harmonizing removes.
  • From space: below the calendar, pick a month and its fire detections appear over NASA satellite imagery of that month’s peak fire day. The imagery is true color from NASA GIBS.
  • NOAA-20/21 forward link: Suomi NPP data end on 2 November 2026. Per-region day/night ratios convert NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 detections into S-NPP equivalents, extending the record to 14 November 2026. The ratios were fitted on 2018–2023 data and tested on 2024–2026 data.
  • Downloads: every chart can be saved as a picture, and the data can be downloaded as CSV for any date range and map box. The same CSVs are served at /api/hotspots and /api/series.
  • Proof on unseen years: the model is trained on 2012–2019 and scored on 2020–2025 against what VIIRS actually counted. The scores are shown on the ledger and the method page. Ghana’s error was 4.3%, against 6.8% for one constant ratio; in NW India the ratio wins (3.2% vs. 7.3%), and the page publishes that result.
  • World scoreboard (/method#scoreboard): in every country, our model is tested against one simple constant ratio. Where the ratio did better, the site publishes the ratio. The model won in 92 of 176 countries; seven, however, are too sparse to check.
  • Independent check (/method#referee): fire detections are compared with MODIS burned area before and after 2012, as a check that does not depend on our model. The 2012 jump in detections per km² burned is 2.2–4.6× in the stitched record and 0.84–1.04× in the harmonized record.
  • Satellite drift: shows how the Terra and Aqua overpass times have drifted, and why that changes the share of each day’s fire that MODIS sees. Terra now passes about 1.5 hours earlier and Aqua about 1.5 hours later than during training, so recent MODIS data are less reliable.
  • Accessible charts: charts can be read with the keyboard (arrow keys step through values), and each one has a text description for screen readers.
  • Was it the weather?: the site compares high- and low-fire months against top-quarter fire weather.

Fire Ledger gives the world its first consistent satellite fire record by harmonizing VIIRS and MODIS data. The raw record artificially inflated trends: when VIIRS replaced MODIS in 2012, it jumped by about four times even though the fire itself didn’t change. With MODIS now ending, the 2001–2011 years would otherwise be impossible to compare with anything measured today. By translating those years onto the VIIRS scale with our model, and then carrying the record past Suomi NPP’s end with NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, Fire Ledger rescues 11 years of fire history. Our project changes the conclusions that can be drawn from this data. Stitched naively, Ghana’s fires appear to rise 5.1% a year, but after harmonization this rise disappears, revealing that it was an artifact of the switch from MODIS to VIIRS. The tool lets researchers in 176 countries ask practical questions against a fair baseline while considering factors such as weather and human activity. In NW India, for example, this season was the quietest in 26 years even though the weather was more fire-prone than usual, which points to a change in human burning rather than in the climate. The site also prioritizes accessibility, with screen-reader support and a layout that works on phones, so that anybody can use it and get something from it.
